**The Sorrows of Young Werther**
Goethe's 1774 epistolary novel and a defining work of the Sturm und Drang movement. The sensitive young Werther, staying in the village of Wahlheim, falls hopelessly in love with Lotte (Charlotte), who is engaged to and then marries the sensible Albert, and he finally shoots himself. The book made Goethe famous and was blamed for a wave of copycat suicides across Europe.

**Ossian, the pistols, and the linden trees**
Key scenes from Werther's ending. On their last evening Werther reads Lotte his translation of the Gaelic "Ossian" poems, and they kiss passionately; he then borrows Albert's pistols, saying he is "going on a journey," and shoots himself. He asks to be buried in a corner of the churchyard between two linden (lime) trees. Earlier, Lotte and Werther bond when she says the name of the poet "Klopstock" during a storm, and Werther says the only book that calms him is Homer.

**Faust and Mephistopheles**
Goethe's two-part closet drama, his masterpiece. It opens with a "Prologue in Heaven" in which God allows Mephistopheles to tempt the scholar Faust. Mephistopheles first follows Faust home from an Easter walk as a black poodle; Faust, who struggles to translate the opening of the Gospel of John, signs a pact in blood, wagering his soul that he will never wish to stay in a moment forever.

**Gretchen (Margarete)**
The young woman Faust seduces in Part One. Faust and Mephistopheles kill her brother Valentine, a soldier; a sleeping potion Faust gives her accidentally kills her mother; and she drowns her newborn child and is imprisoned. At the end of Part One a voice from above declares her "saved" (redeemed). She sings the ballad of the "King in Thule," and Part One also includes the scene in Auerbach's Cellar in Leipzig and Faust's dull assistant Wagner.

**Faust, Part Two**
The second part, finished shortly before Goethe's death in 1832. Wagner creates the artificial man Homunculus, Faust is united with Helen of Troy and has a son named Euphorion with her, and in the end angels carry Faust's soul away so that Mephistopheles fails to claim it. The drama closes with the "Chorus Mysticus," ending with the "Eternal Feminine" drawing us upward.

**Elective Affinities**
Goethe's 1809 novel that compares human relationships to a chemical double displacement reaction ("AB plus CD yields AD plus BC"). The married couple Eduard and Charlotte invite the Captain (Otto) and the young Ottilie to their estate; Eduard falls for Ottilie and Charlotte for the Captain, and the child they conceive in "spiritual adultery" resembles both Ottilie and the Captain.

**Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship**
Goethe's novel often considered the first Bildungsroman. Wilhelm leaves his merchant background to join a troupe of actors, adopts the mysterious girl Mignon, helps stage Shakespeare's Hamlet, at one point dresses as a count and is taken for his double, and finally joins the secret Society of the Tower and marries Natalie. It was preceded by Wilhelm Meister's Theatrical Calling and followed by Wilhelm Meister's Journeyman Years, in which Wilhelm takes his son Felix to the "Pedagogical Province."

**"The Erlking" ("Erlkönig")**
Goethe's ballad, later set to music by Schubert, which begins "Who rides, so late, through night and wind?" A father rides home with his son, who asks "why do you hide your face in fear?" The boy sees the Erlking, who promises that his daughters will "rock you, and dance, and sing you to sleep," while the father dismisses these visions as fog and wind; when they reach home, the child is dead in his arms.

**Italian Journey and the Roman Elegies**
Goethe's account of his 1786–88 travels in Italy, which includes his time with the painter Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein (who painted the famous portrait of Goethe in the Roman countryside). The trip also inspired the erotic Roman Elegies, a cycle of 24 poems.

**Egmont**
Goethe's tragedy about Count Egmont, a Flemish noble and Knight of the Golden Fleece who opposes Spanish Catholic rule in the Netherlands alongside Count Horn. He is arrested and executed by the Duke of Alba, while his beloved Klärchen poisons herself. Beethoven wrote incidental music for the play.

**Weimar, Karl August, and Friedrich Schiller**
Goethe spent most of his life in Weimar, serving Duke Karl August as a privy councilor. With his close friend Friedrich Schiller he founded Weimar Classicism; Goethe planned a work on William Tell but gave the subject to Schiller, who wrote the play.

**Theory of Colours and Metamorphosis of Plants**
Goethe's scientific works. Metamorphosis of Plants (1790) argued that the various organs of plants are homologous transformations of the leaf, and Theory of Colours (1810) studied human color perception, opposing Newton's optics.

**Poetry and Truth and Goethe's life**
Goethe's autobiography, Poetry and Truth (Dichtung und Wahrheit), written over about two decades, with its last part published after his death. It covers his early life, including his romance with Friederike Brion in Sessenheim, which inspired early poems, and his love for Charlotte Buff, who was engaged to Johann Kestner; they were the models for Lotte and Albert in Werther. Rüdiger Safranski's biography is subtitled "Life as a Work of Art," and Emerson's Representative Men chose Goethe as "the Writer."

**West-Eastern Divan and the "Marienbad Elegy"**
West-Eastern Divan is Goethe's late poetry collection inspired by the Persian poet Hafez. The "Marienbad Elegy" was written after the elderly Goethe's marriage proposal to the young Ulrike von Levetzow was rejected.

**Torquato Tasso, The Natural Daughter, and "Heidenröslein"**
Other Goethe works. Torquato Tasso is a play about the Renaissance Italian poet; The Natural Daughter follows Eugenie, who is abducted on the orders of the Duke's Secretary; his early plays include The Lover's Caprice and The Triumph of Sensibility. The poem "Heidenröslein" ("Little Rose on the Heath") tells of a boy who picks a wild rose that pricks him in self-defense.
